publication: Determinism and Freedom in Stoic Philosophy (Clarendon Press, Oxford; copyright 1998, paperback 2001)
stance: NO — the early Stoics had no notion of free will in the modern (libertarian) sense
position_summary: The pivotal NO. Zeno, Cleanthes and Chrysippus developed (1) universal teleological causal determinism, (2) a causal theory of moral responsibility via the cylinder analogy, and (3) a concept of to eph' hēmin = di' hēmōn ('that which comes about through us', one-sided causative). The modern free-will problem (compatibilism vs incompatibilism, alternative possibilities decoupled from universal causation) is anachronistic for the classical Stoa. Methodological priority: reconstruct the problems the Stoics actually faced within their own ontology, not read the modern debate back into the sources.
contested_locus: Chrysippus cylinder analogy (Cicero, De Fato 39-44 + Gellius, NA 7.2.11), synkatathesis (assent), to eph' hēmin
attested_quote: "under the surface of superficial resemblance to modern discussions of the free-will problem ... a very different ontological framework lurks" (Bobzien 2001:277-280); "The topic of determinism and freedom lies at the very heart of Stoic philosophy in that it provides an essential link between its three basic parts: ethics, physics, and logic" (2001:296-298)

publication: The Inadvertent Conception and Late Birth of the Free-Will Problem (Phronesis XLIII/2, Brill)
stance: NO — the free-will problem was not discovered but inadvertently constructed in the 2nd c. CE; earliest unambiguous awareness is Alexander of Aphrodisias
position_summary: Complements the 2001 monograph. The 'discovery' of the problem of causal determinism and freedom of decision results from a conflation (mix-up) of Aristotelian and Stoic thought in later antiquity, no later than the early 2nd c. CE. Distinguishes two conceptions of eph' hēmin: (a) Stoic = one-sided causative (causal responsibility, no implied power to do otherwise); (b) later Peripatetic/Platonist (Alexander) = two-sided potestative (real power to do or not do otherwise, indeterminist). Two conceptions of moral responsibility: MR1 (autonomy of the agent, held by the Stoics) vs MR2 (ability to do otherwise, toward which Alexander moves).
contested_locus: to eph' hēmin (one-sided causative vs two-sided potestative); Alexander of Aphrodisias, De Fato; transition eph' hēmin → autexousion
attested_quote: "the 'discovery' of the problem of causal determinism and freedom of decision in Greek philosophy is the result of a mix-up of Aristotelian and Stoic thought in later antiquity" (Bobzien 1998:22-25); "The earliest unambiguous evidence for the awareness of any kind of 'free-will problem' occurs in Alexander of Aphrodisias" (1998:187-189); "There is in this model no space for free will (i.e. for a decision making faculty that is causally independent of the mind's individual nature)" (1998:498-499)

publication: A Free Will: Origins of the Notion in Ancient Thought (ed. A. A. Long, foreword D. Sedley; University of California Press, Sather Classical Lectures 68)
page: ch. 2 (Aristotle, no will), ch. 3-6 (Stoics, Epictetus), esp. the chapter 'Epictetus and the first notion of a will'
stance: QUALIFIED YES (developmental) — the EARLY Stoics did not yet have a free will, but Stoicism is the tradition that first developed the notion; it was LATER Stoicism (Epictetus) that produced the first identifiable notion of a free will
position_summary: Against Dihle 1982 (who credited Augustine). The notion of a free will is a technical philosophical notion with an identifiable historical origin, not a perennial human belief. Neither Plato nor Aristotle had a notion of will or free will. The Stoics' theory of will emerges from the theory of assent (synkatathesis) to impressions (phantasiai); prohairesis in Epictetus becomes the locus of moral agency. Epictetus, by enriching the early Stoic theory of assent with a developed notion of an inner life, articulated 'our first actual notion of a free will' — though only the wise person truly possesses it. This Stoic notion passed into Christian doctrine, especially via Origen. So Frede agrees with Bobzien that the EARLY Stoa lacked free will, but unlike Bobzien locates a genuine (not merely inadvertent/anachronistic) emergence of free will within the Stoic tradition itself, in Epictetus.
contested_locus: synkatathesis (assent to phantasiai); prohairesis in Epictetus; to autexousion; eleutheria; the term autexousion (twice in Musonius fr., then Epictetus)
attested_quote: "The notion of a free will is a notion we have inherited from antiquity. It was first in antiquity that one came to think of human beings as having a free will." (Frede 2011:328-330); "So here we have our first actual notion of a free will. It is a notion of a will such that there is no power or force in the world which could prevent it from making the choices one needs to make to live a good life" (2011:2770-2773); "The term [autexousion] is twice found in the fragments of Musonius and then more often in Epictetus. It comes to be used by Platonists and Peripatetics but also from Justin Martyr onwards very frequently by Christian authors." (2011:2690-2695)

publication: L'idée de volonté dans le stoïcisme (Presses Universitaires de France, Paris)
page: n/a — PDF in library is an image scan without a usable text layer (no OCR); page-specific quotes could not be transcribed
stance: YES (proto-volition) — the early Stoics elaborated an 'idea of will' (volonté), located in hormē (impulse) and synkatathesis (assent), well before any Christian or late-antique 'discovery'
position_summary: The classic French monograph arguing that a genuine concept of will (volonté) is already present and systematically elaborated in early Stoicism, grounded in the doctrine of impulse (hormē) and rational assent (synkatathesis) to impressions — i.e. the will as the hēgemonikon's rational consent. This is the position later contested by Dihle 1982 (will = invention of Augustine) and reframed by Frede 2011 (full notion of free will only with Epictetus) and Bobzien (no free will / no two-sided potestative eph' hēmin in the early Stoa). Voelke is the standard pre-Bobzien reference for reading volition into the early Stoa. NOTE: position summarised from the work's established thesis and its role in the secondary literature; the library PDF has no extractable text, so no verbatim quotation is supplied (integrity policy).
contested_locus: hormē (impulse), synkatathesis (assent), hēgemonikon; the notion of 'volonté' itself

publication: Ethics and Human Action in Early Stoicism (Clarendon Press, Oxford)
page: 66-70 (Cleanthes' Hymn / 'free will' reading rejected), 88-89 (Alexander vs Stoic eph' hēmin)
stance: NO free will — Stoic to eph' hēmin concerns assent and voluntariness grounded in moral responsibility, NOT a libertarian power to do otherwise
position_summary: Moral responsibility is the central, characteristic problem of early Stoic moral philosophy. Chrysippus reconciles responsibility with fate by making assent a special internal cause that grounds attribution to the agent. Inwood explicitly rejects the reading of Cleanthes' Hymn lines as a reference to an autonomous 'free will': it would be absurd for bad men to be free of the causal chain in a way good men are not; 'without you' refers to normative deviation from Right Reason (Zeus), not to libertarian freedom. He stresses that Alexander of Aphrodisias' definition of to eph' hēmin (the power to do either of two opposite actions after deliberation) is explicitly NOT what the Stoics meant — Alexander imports an alien, anti-Stoic premise. Converges with Bobzien on the one-sided/causative reading of Stoic eph' hēmin.
contested_locus: Cleanthes, Hymn to Zeus (the 'without you nothing comes to be' lines); synkatathesis (assent); to eph' hēmin; Alexander of Aphrodisias, De Fato (p. 180.5-7 Bruns)
attested_quote: "These lines have been interpreted as a reference to an autonomous 'free will'. But this must be wrong. For it would be strange indeed if bad men were thought to be free of the chain of cause and effect in a way that good men are not." (Inwood 1985:70); "[Alexander] bases his argument on the presumption that 'what is in our power' (to eph' hêmin) is that which enables a man to do either of two opposite actions in a given circumstance... He knows that this is not what the Stoics mean by to eph' hêmin and that neither of his presumptions is part of the Stoic analysis of responsible action." (1985:88-89)

publication: The Stoic Life: Emotions, Duties, and Fate (Clarendon Press, Oxford)
stance: NO free will / compatibilism — Chrysippus is a compatibilist ('soft determinist'); 'up to us' means originating from one's own character, fully compatible with fate
position_summary: Reconstructs Chrysippus' reply to the determinist argument that 'if everything happens by fate, nothing is up to us'. Chrysippus rejects the premise that the cause of impulse not being up to us makes the impulse not up to us: there are two causes, and the external impression is by far the less important; assent is the major cause and IS up to us. Via the cylinder-and-cone analogy, actions are 'up to us' because they originate from our own character and dispositions (however we came to have them) — the causal chain of 'up-to-us-ness' terminates in our present character, not behind it. Brennan explicitly applies the modern label: 'We usually call this sort of a position a compatibilist position, or a soft-determinist position', contrasting it with incompatibilists (libertarians and hard determinists). External compulsion excuses; fate working through one's own psychology does not. No notion of libertarian free will is attributed to the Stoics.
contested_locus: Chrysippus cylinder-and-cone analogy (Cicero, De Fato 41-43; Gellius, NA 7.2); the Lazy/Idle Argument premise 'if everything by fate, nothing up to us'; synkatathesis (assent); to eph' hēmin ('up to us')
attested_quote: "According to the Stoics, my actions, impulses and assents are all caused and determined by Fate, and they are also 'up to me', and these two claims are perfectly compatible with one another. We usually call this sort of a position a 'compatibilist' position, or a 'soft determinist' position." (Brennan 2005:256); "Our actions are 'up to us' because they originate from our impulses and assents. And those are 'up to us' because they originate from our character and dispositions, from our minds and the 'shapes' they currently have." (2005:255-256)

publication: The Stoics on Determinism and Compatibilism (Ashgate, Aldershot)
stance: NO free will / compatibilism — the Stoics were both determinists and compatibilists; prior necessitation does not by itself preclude genuine desert of praise or blame
position_summary: Frames the Stoics as determinists (every state and event, including our actions and their psychology, is necessitated by prior causes) AND compatibilists (necessitation does not on its own cancel responsibility). They depart from BOTH the hard-determinist/eliminativist position (already active in antiquity) AND the libertarian/anti-determinist (Epicureans early, Alexander of Aphrodisias late). Develops the role of reflection in Chrysippus' psychology of action and distinguishes three compatibilist theories of Chrysippus (T1/T2/T3). On Epictetus, Salles reads responsibility for unreflective action within the same causal/compatibilist framework. In Destrée/Salles/Zingano (eds.) 2014, ch. 'Epictetus and the causal conception of moral responsibility and what is eph' hēmin' he defends a CAUSAL reading of Epictetan eph' hēmin in continuity with Chrysippus — explicitly resisting Frede's reading of Epictetus as the inventor of a free will.
contested_locus: Chrysippus' three compatibilist theories (T1-T3); cylinder analogy; reflection and the psychology of action; Epictetus on to eph' hēmin (Diss.); the Idle/Lazy Argument (Cicero, De Fato 28-30)
attested_quote: "The Stoics themselves were determinists: on their view, every state and event ... is necessitated by prior causes. But they were also compatibilists, that is, they contended that prior necessitation does not preclude on its own that we genuinely deserve praise or blame for the actions we perform." (Salles 2005:xiii)

stance: Compatibilist / continuist — defends the internal coherence of Chrysippus on fate and responsibility; reads Epictetan prohairesis carefully (neither a modern 'free will' nor reducible to mere decision), within the Stoic causal framework
position_summary: Specialist of Stoic logic and the doctrine of fate (Le Centre Léon Robin). Defends a fine exegetical reading of Stoic compatibilism and the internal coherence of Chrysippus on destiny and moral responsibility — against the charge of incoherence. On Epictetus, analyses prohairesis as moral 'decision/will' or the 'moral person', cautioning against anachronistically equating it with the modern free will (a measured position between Bobzien's strict NO and Frede's 'first free will in Epictetus').
